newsitem.title: USA: Justice Dept. urges barring SBC long-distance plan.
newsitem.headline: Justice Dept. urges barring SBC long-distance plan.

text.p: The Justice Department Friday urged the Federal Communications Commission to reject a bid by regional Bell company SBC Communications Inc. to sell long-distance service in Oklahoma.
The department said SBC, the parent of Southwestern Bell, should be prohibited from offering long-distance service until its monopoly opens to competing local services.
The law requires that the FCC give "substantial weight" to the Justice Department recommendation.
SBC filed its application with the FCC on April 11 to get a slice of the $80 billion domestic long-distance business. The FCC must act on the application by July 10.
"New competitors still don't have a real opportunity to compete in Oklahoma's local telephone markets," said Joel Klein, acting assistant attorney general, calling the application "premature."

"Opening up local markets under the Telecommunications Act will enable consumers to reap the significant benefits that competition will bring -- lower prices, higher quality service and increased service offerings," Klein said in a statement.
The 1996 communications law passed by Congress permits SBC and other local Bell companies to enter the long-distance market only afer meeting a 14-point checklist showing they have real competition.
In a statement, SBC expressed its disappointment.

"We are naturally disappointed," the company said in a statement from its headquarters in San Antonio, Texas. "We remain as confident as ever that we have done everything required under the law to open our markets to companies wishing to offer long distance service."
SBC Chief Executive Officer Edward Whitacre said last month his company already has local competition.

"There are 90 companies approved to provide local service in our service area and they are doing it," he told Reuters after the company's annual meeting. "If they say they are not, I can prove they are."
The Justice Department was not convinced, however, that any company is providing residential service in competition with SBC.
The bid was opposed by a the Association for Local Telecommunications Services, a group of 33 companies offering local service in competition with the regional Bell companies.
Before the decision was reached, the association called the SBC application "frivolous and premature."
SBC stock edged up 12.5 cents to $57.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
